job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Zoe Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Pretty full. I'm up at seven, I do an hour on my newsletter, which is a weekly money guide for students, and then I apply for jobs with a mix of AI help and my own editing. In the afternoon I have calls with people in fintech, coffee chats mostly. I live in Ashgrove with my mum, who is a nurse, and my auntie Ngozi, so dinner is always loud.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you study, and what was your internship?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Finance and economics, good result. I did six weeks at a small fintech start-up in customer onboarding, mostly checking identity documents and fixing mistakes in the account set-up. I use AI every day, for summarising reports, drafting emails, building models, and I like to find the edges of what it gets wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, and I'd quietly feel a bit let down, because I like the tools. To my friends I'd say the useful bits are still useful, so don't throw them out. In my newsletter I'd write a calm piece saying the hype was too loud but the habits are worth keeping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means the competition for entry jobs is the usual crowd. My edge, being good with the tools, still counts but less, because everyone slows down to the same pace. I'm not worried, though, because I already have a few leads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the newsletter going, aim for 2,000 subscribers by spring, and keep doing a coffee chat a week with people in fintech. I'd apply for about ten roles a week, mostly in product operations, risk or analysis. I'd put time into a small portfolio on my site, including a model of student loan costs, so employers can see what I can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relaxed. Not thrilled, but it doesn't scare me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the newsletter do for your job hunt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What does the newsletter do for your job hunt?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you run it full time if it grew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's proof I can explain money to normal people. A hiring manager at a payments company told me the newsletter was the reason she replied to my application. I'd keep writing it even if I got a job, because it's mine.

say: I'd say fair enough and write a calm newsletter piece: **the hype was loud** but the habits are worth keeping.
I'd tell friends not to throw the tools out.
think: Competition for entry jobs is the usual crowd, and my **edge** with tools counts a bit less.
I'm not worried: I already have a few leads.
do: Grow the newsletter to **2,000 subscribers** by spring.
Apply for about ten roles a week and keep one coffee chat a week.
Build a **portfolio** with a student loan cost model.

steps.text: Grow the money newsletter to 2,000 subscribers by spring
Apply for ten roles a week in operations and risk
Add a student loan cost model to my website

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening, so get good at it. At the start-up I'd tell them the most useful people will be the ones who can check what the tools produce. In my newsletter I'd write about which entry jobs are changing and what a graduate can do about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think a lot of entry roles get cut or merged, including onboarding, which I did on my internship. But I'd also say the people who can combine finance, tools and clear writing are in demand. I'm lucky to be in that group, and I know that doesn't make everyone safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to roles that say AI-assisted or operations in the title, and ask to be put on the team that tests tools. I'd take on two freelance clients writing financial explainers. I'd also take a short certificate in data analysis, and I'd keep some of my savings for a gap between contracts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. A bit of adrenaline, which I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a friend who isn't comfortable with the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you say to a friend who isn't comfortable with the tools?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you choose between a job and freelance clients?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit with her for an hour, open the tool and ask it to do something she cares about, like her CV or her rent budget. People learn when it helps with their own thing. I've done that with three friends, and two of them now use it daily.

say: I'd say it's happening, so get good at it, and the most useful people **check the outputs**.
I'd write a newsletter piece on which entry jobs are changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have to move quickly on training and support, and I'd back whatever gives people a floor to stand on. At the start-up I'd tell them they should work out which jobs are truly safe. In my newsletter I'd write a piece on what to do with your money if your income might change fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's hard for everyone, me included. If the software does any thinking work, a fintech doesn't need a grad doing onboarding or analysis. But I'm also fast, I'd move first, and I have people in my corner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to land anything with people or decisions in it, like client success or a regulated job where a person must sign. I'd put my newsletter forward as a business and try to get paid sponsorships. I'd also cut spending on anything extra and keep my savings at six months. And I'd talk with my mum and auntie about what we'd do if my income didn't appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and wired. I'd be doing a lot, and I'd also be afraid I'd picked the wrong thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the wrong thing you're afraid of picking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What's the wrong thing you're afraid of picking?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you talk to your mum and auntie Ngozi about money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anything built on the idea that being quick with tools is rare. In two years everyone will be quick with the tools, so I'm trying to sell what's still scarce, which is trust and being known. I just don't know if that's enough.

say: I'd say we need training and a **floor** to stand on, and write a newsletter piece on money when income may change.
I'd tell the start-up to work out which jobs are truly safe.

It's hard for everyone, me included.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to do something clever and short enough that you'd be silly to wait. I'd tell the start-up they need to start training now. In my newsletter I'd write a long piece on a five-year money plan for graduates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd see it as a race with a head start. If I get a job in the next year and keep building the newsletter, I'd have four years of experience and a name. That could be my safety. But I'd also be watching how things go, because the plan could fall apart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a job in fintech by the end of this winter, build skills in risk and product, and run the newsletter on the side. I'd save about a third of my pay. By year three I'd either start a small advisory business or move into a role where a person must make the call. I'd also learn a bit about regulation, because it's slower to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, mostly. Focused, and a bit alert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you learn regulation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Why learn regulation?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you drop the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because laws move slowly, and the people who understand the rules will be needed longer. If I'm the person who knows what the software is allowed to do, I'm useful for longer than I would be knowing how to use it.

say: I'd say five years is long enough to do something clever and short enough that **waiting** is silly.
I'd write a long piece on a five-year money plan.

The plan could still fall apart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift. I'd say to people, plan like a career still exists and also plan for it to change. In my newsletter I'd write about saving, buying assets, and building more than one source of income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm excited. Ten years is enough to build a real career or a real business, and I'd have a decade of experience before the end point. I'd still keep an eye on how fast things move, because ten years often ends up being six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a job in fintech this year, get my professional qualification by 26, and grow the newsletter into a proper media brand. I'd buy a small flat with my savings by 28, and I'd invest every month. And I'd help my auntie Ngozi set up her small catering business with proper accounts, because that's something I can do right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Light and ambitious. It's the one picture where I'd make big plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the media brand look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would the media brand look like?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you help auntie Ngozi's catering business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small team, two or three writers, a podcast, and clear paid tiers. I'd keep the human voice at the front, since people trust a person more than a feed. If the tools can write a thousand articles, I'd want people to still pick mine.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift**: plan for a career to exist and also to change.
I'd write about saving, assets and multiple incomes.
think: Ten years is enough to build a real career or business, but it often ends up being **six**.
I'm excited, with an eye on the speed.
do: Take a fintech job this year and get a **professional qualification** by 26.
Grow the newsletter into a paid **media brand**.
Buy a small flat by 28 and invest monthly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, because speed with tools stops being rare in two years and I'd have to sell something else. What would help is quick public training for people who aren't tool people, and clear rules about where a human must sign off.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I sound confident, and I am, but I hold it lightly. A lot of what I do depends on being early, and being early only works once.

headlineQuote: A lot of what I do depends on being early, and being early only works once.
portrait: Zoe is 23, a finance graduate from Ashgrove, living with her nurse mother and auntie Ngozi, with **no offer yet**.
She uses AI every day, runs a student money **newsletter** and does weekly coffee chats in fintech.
Her centre views make her practical: public floors, training and clear sign-off rules.
She teaches friends the tools, and plans to sell trust and regulation knowledge once speed is common.
She is calm in slow scenarios and **uneasy** in fast ones, aware her edge may not last.
biggestWorry: The **AGI by 2028** picture worries her most, because speed with tools stops being rare.
whatWouldHelp: Quick **public training** for people who aren't tool people.
Clear rules about where a human must sign off.
